name: Hana Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for having me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties. What you say is confidential, so you can tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think. Could you tell me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I teach the Reception class at Ashby Green Primary, a small church school in a village, so my children are four and five years old. There are only sixty-two children in the whole school and eighteen in my class. A day is phonics, counting with blocks, painting, lots of outdoor play, shoelaces, nose-wiping and the odd tears at the gate. It's my second year, and I still go home some days covered in glitter.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The paperwork that comes with the little ones. Every child has a learning journal where I log observations, photos and notes for parents, and there's a big assessment at the end of the year. I've started using an AI tool now and then to tidy up my notes, after the deputy head showed me. The other hard part is that the school's numbers are falling, and there's been talk of merging with the bigger school in town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, children need people, not programmes, and I'd be glad we didn't throw everything at it. I'd say it to the other mums and dads at the school gate too. I'd keep using the tool for notes because it does save time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, AI isn't my worry in that world; the school roll is. If we drop below fifty-five children, the diocese might merge us with Church Lane in town, and the newest teacher is the one who has to reapply. My husband Lukas is a carpenter, so he's busy, but we've only got about three months saved because we just paid for our wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep teaching and keep using the AI tool for the learning journals, which saves me maybe two hours a week. I'd help with the school's open mornings to bring new families in. And Lukas and I would rebuild our savings, about £200 a month, before we think about a baby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. The school feels fragile, even if AI doesn't change anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the parents at the open morning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them what we have that a big school doesn't. At a small village school, a child is known by name by every adult in the building. I'd show them the vegetable patch the Reception class planted and the photos of the harvest festival.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the merger happened, what would you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply for a post at Church Lane, and I think there'd be one, but it's a much bigger school. Lukas says I'd be fine anywhere, but I chose a village school for a reason. I'd miss knowing every family.

say: I'd say **children need people**, not programmes.
I'd keep using the **AI note tool** because it does save time.
think: My real worry is the **school roll** and a possible merger.
With **three months** saved after our wedding, we're not very cushioned.
do: Keep using the AI tool for **learning journals**, saving two hours a week.
Help run **open mornings** to bring in new families.
Rebuild savings by **£200 a month** before thinking about a baby.
feel: **Uneasy**, because the **school feels fragile** even without AI.

steps.text: Keep using the AI tool to tidy learning journal notes
Help run open mornings to attract new Reception families
Rebuild savings by £200 a month with Lukas

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's useful for paperwork and planning, and it would be daft not to use it for that. But I'd also say you can't teach a four-year-old to hold a pencil with a computer. I'd say both, and mean both.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think Reception is one of the safest places in a school, because it's mostly hands-on: toilets, coats, cuddles, sand trays. The parts that change are the journals and the assessments, which honestly I'd be glad to hand over. My worry is still the falling roll, not AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the AI tools properly once the deputy head and the other teachers are using them, probably by the spring term. I'd use the time saved for the children who need extra help with speech, which is a lot of them since the pandemic. And we'd keep saving, maybe start trying for a baby in a year or two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly about the school, not the technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone at school you'd worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mrs Patel in the office, who does the bookings, the dinner money and the letters home. That's exactly the kind of thing this takes over. She's been there twenty years and knows every family, and I'd hate to see her go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You sound calm about your own job. Why uneasy then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because a small school needs every adult to stay open. If the office goes and the teaching assistant hours go, there's less of a school left to save. And then the merger talk gets louder.

think: Reception is **mostly hands-on**, so it's one of the safest places.

steps.text: Learn the school's AI tools properly by the spring term

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to slow down and protect children, and I'd say it at church, at school and to anyone who'd listen. I'd say families should be the ones deciding how their children are taught. I'd be calmer in public than I felt inside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the thinking side of my job goes by 2028, which is fine, it's paperwork. But in 2031 the robots come, and Reception is hands-on work. I don't believe parents would hand their four-year-olds to a robot, but councils might try it to save money. And if the school's already under pressure, it might be easier to close it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the AI tools for everything I can by 2028 to show I'm efficient. I'd do a course in early years special needs, because children with extra needs will always need a person. And Lukas and I would talk seriously about whether to wait on a baby, and cut back so we've got six months saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's the robots part that gets me, more than the AGI part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the 2031 date mean for Lukas?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lukas is a carpenter, so he's hands-on too. Both of us would get those three extra years, which is something. But if both of us were at risk from 2031, I'd want to be ready before then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the parents of your Reception children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them their children need a person who loves them while they learn. I'd tell them to fight for that. Parents in a village like ours would fight, I'm sure of that.

say: I'd say we must **protect children** and slow down.
I'd say **families should decide** how their children are taught.
think: The **paperwork side** goes by 2028, which I'd be fine with.
**Robots in 2031** worry me, because councils might try them to save money.

S2.quote: Children need a person who loves them while they learn.
fieldNote: Both she and her carpenter husband do **hands-on work**, so 2031 is their date.

steps.text: Use AI for all learning journals and assessments by 2028
Take a course in early years special educational needs
Build savings to six months with Lukas
Delay trying for a baby until after 2028

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have time to get it right, and that schools should use it to make sure little ones still have people around them. I'd join the parents' group pushing to keep our school open. I'd sound measured.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is enough time for me to get good at the job and get the special needs training. Robots wouldn't come until about 2034, which feels a long way away. By then, I'd hope the school is either safe or I've moved to something even more people-based.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the special needs course over two years, part-time. I'd use the AI tools as they become normal at school. And Lukas and I would probably still start trying for a baby, maybe next year, because waiting forever isn't living.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but steadier. I can see a path.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'waiting forever isn't living'. Can you say more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum always says there's never a perfect time. If I waited until I knew what AI would do, I'd be forty. Lukas and I want a family, and we'd make it work with what we have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the school safer in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: More families moving to the village, honestly. If housing was cheaper, young couples would stay, and the roll would go up. That's not about AI, but it's what decides whether my job exists.

I'd join the **parents' group** fighting to keep our school open.
think: Five years is enough to get the **special needs training** done.
**Robots by 2034** feel a long way off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and we should plan carefully, as families and as a village. I'd say children still need people, and I'd mean it with confidence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years is good for me. By 2036 I'd be thirty-seven, maybe with a child at school myself, and the robots come around 2039. I'd have time to become a properly good early years teacher, maybe lead the early years side. The roll is still my worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep teaching, do the special needs training, and use AI for the paperwork. Lukas and I would have a baby in the next couple of years. We'd save towards buying a house in the village, so we can stay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a little, but mostly settled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want for your own child in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want them to learn to work with their hands, like Lukas, and to know how to look after people. And I'd want them to go to a small school where everyone knows their name.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does anything about ten years make you more worried?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only that people might get complacent. Ten years sounds like forever, and then it's here. I'd want us to use it, not waste it.

say: I'd say **ten years** is time to plan as families and as a village.
I'd say with confidence that **children still need people**.
think: By 2036 I could **lead early years**, with robots not until 2039.
The **school roll** is still my main worry.
do: Keep teaching and finish the **special needs training**.
Have a **baby** in the next couple of years.
Save to **buy a house** in the village.
S4.quote: Ten years sounds like forever, and then it's here.
fieldNote: Ten years makes her picture **leading early years**.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because of what it does by 2031. My job is hands-on, and so is Lukas's, and three years isn't long. What would help is clear rules that young children are always taught by people, and support for small village schools to stay open.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: About small schools. Everyone talks about big changes, but a lot of what decides people's lives is local: housing, buses, whether a school stays open. AI is just one more thing on top.
